rv.q: Every move she makes is precise, vital, mesmerising.
Gough is flinty and fierce and utterly compelling as she descends into derangement.
Her unravelling is painful to watch, and her performance really does rise to the heights of Greek drama, intense and unstoppably tragic.

His version is a serious, if overstylised, inquiry into the American classic, lifting the drama from its original east coast setting and transposing it to the deep south, several decades later, in the early 1900s.
But it also slows down what is already an overloaded, circular text and proceeds at such a high pitch that, after a while, it’s beset by a sense of diminishing returns.
A fascinating but fussy and ultimately slightly misguided take on a rarely performed classic that worked better when Gough Snr starred.
While it confirms Bamgboye’s flair for dramatic staging - he was nominated for the Standard’s 2025. Emerging Talent theatre award - this show is frankly overwrought.
In this production, recognisable human passions come a distant second to glossy presentation.
The musical, physical and theatrical artistry is so vibrantly clear in this performance that the story almost fades into an experimental backdrop for exploring the violence of desire.
This revival lives and breathes through the temperature of its performances, with Gough’s Abbie and Momoh’s Eben ensuring the farm’s suffocating heat feels palpable.

He throws everything at an expressionistic, visceral production that is always gripping – but all its inventiveness and commitment can’t quite raise the play to the level of insight that truly great O’Neill can achieve.

The latest foray by the Almeida Theatre into the far corners of the American repertory has come up with a reviewer’s nightmare: a striking, expressionist production, inventively and forcefully performed, of a dismal and dispiriting rural tragedy.
Desire Under the Elms is well acted with stunning lighting and focused direction.
But while you can’t help admire his heated, guttural vision, it stretches out the play’s action and ultimately threatens to overwhelm the drama it seeks to illuminate.
Exaggeration is the show's downfall. Every scene begins at maximum pitch with the performers gesticulating and shouting out their lines in a frenzied panic.
Indeed the 2 hour and 40 minutes running time (including interval) vastly outstays its welcome.
This Desire Under The Elms is a stunning composition, driven by unbridled talent and passion.
Gough’s performance will be talked about for years to come - and rightly so.
For a playwright whose work can sometimes feel like an endurance test, this is a gripping, taut and excellently conceived piece.
Bamgboye makes them immediate not through explanation but through sound, bodies and charged silences.
The project is largely successful and at no time does Bamgboye distort the emotional truth of the writing.
Bamgboye’s production strives for new meaning and sometimes succeeds, but often his modern staging and naturalist characters feel at odds with O’Neill’s archaic dialogue and domestic drama.

Now, former Almeida Resident Director Ebenezer Bamgboye revitalises its taboo elements by transplanting it to the Deep South in the early 1900s in a production which is seismically visceral but equally enervating.
Bamgboye’s production features a bewildering mix of bronze lighting, intrusive music, shouting and random dance sequences which obscure any meaning or message behind the classic.
Though it is admirable in its attempts to bring something new to a Eugene O’Neill classic, the result is a confused and underbaked production that wasn’t quite what I desired.

Rather than allowing the characters' passions and conflicts to gather force and lead inexorably towards a tragedy that is both personal and epic, this production repeatedly spells out what should be left to the audience to feel.
It’s hard to imagine American theatre before this indelibly powerful if flawed work. And that it was the greatest American tragedy, indeed play ever written when it opened in 1924.
It has an interesting story at its heart with the potential to shock and move, but it's bogged down with excess dialogue and can't punch through.
I could appreciate the intensity of what was unfolding without always feeling emotionally connected to it.
As a result, Bamgboye’s take misses the point on several levels.

cn.t: Mixed reception for this stylized O'Neill revival: Kelly Gough's performance earns near-universal praise, but Bamgboye's hyper-expressionist direction divides critics—some find it electrifying, others overwrought.
